chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-Husayn ibn Ishaq, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Durust, from one of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent two angels to the people of a city to overturn it upon its inhabitants. So when they arrived at the city, they found a man supplicating to Allah and pleading humbly. One of the angels said to his companion: 'Do you not see this supplicator?' He said: 'I have seen him, but I must proceed with what my Lord has commanded me.' He said: 'No, but I will not do anything until I refer it back to my Lord.' So he returned to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and said: 'O Lord, I arrived at the city and found Your servant so-and-so supplicating to You and pleading to You.' He said: 'Proceed with what I commanded you, for that man has never had his face clouded with anger towards Me at all.'
ai.seo_question: Why did the angels delay destroying the city when they saw a man praying?
ai.summary: In this narrative from *Al-Kafi*, two angels tasked with destroying a city pause to observe a devout servant deeply engaged in supplication, highlighting the power of *du'a* to potentially delay divine decree. God commands them to proceed, noting that the man’s face never showed anger towards Him, implying his piety was pure and not marred by resentment, thus justifying the decree despite his devotion. This reflects the Shia scholarly understanding of how individual righteousness interacts with collective destiny, where sincere worship is recognized even if it does not avert the ultimate judgment.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Al Husayn Bin Iss’haq, from Ali Bin Mahziyar, from Al Nazar Bin Suweyd, from one of his companions, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic Sent two Angels to the people of a city in order to overthrow its inhabitants. So when they both ended up to the city, they found a man supplicating to Allah<sup>azwj</sup>, and he was desperate. So one of the Angels said to his companion: ‘But, do you not see this supplicator?’ So he said: ‘I have seen him, but I must fulfil what my Lord<sup>azwj</sup> has Commanded me with. So he said, ‘No, but I will not do anything until I refer it to Allah<sup>azwj</sup>’. 
So he returned to Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Bless and high, so he said: ‘O Lord<sup>azwj</sup>! I ended up to the city, so I found Your<sup>azwj</sup> so and so servant supplicating to You<sup>azwj</sup> and he was desperate to You<sup>azwj</sup>’. So He<sup>azwj</sup> Said: “Fulfil with what I<sup>azwj</sup> have Commanded you with, for that man did not even frown his face in anger for Me<sup>azwj</sup> at all”’.
en.sarwar: 7. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Ali ibn Asbat from abu Ishaq al-Khurasaniy from certain persons of his people who has said the following: “He (the Imam) has said, ‘Allah, the most Majestic, the most Glorious, sent revelation to Dawud (David), ‘Alayhi al-Salam, that said, ‘I forgave your sins and placed the blame thereof on the Israelites.’

He (Dawud) asked, ‘How can that be, O Lord? You do not do injustice. He (the Lord) replied, ‘Because they did not express disappointment for what you had done.’” (This Hadith is addressed to Dawud but it is meant to apply to others. It is one of the cases where the popular expression, ‘I address you O slave-girl, but you, the neighbor woman listen.’)
